div.p: THE RIVER WEAVER BILL
WITHDRAWAL OF THR "CHURCHId.

The obnoxious clauses in the River Weaver Bill have been withdrawn. By a unanimous vote of the Trustees at a meeting held on Monday last, it was handed to adopt this course and the bill will now go before the /louse of / ornament as a purely financial one. Of course it may happen that the financial policy of the Trustees may be debated and discussed before the Committee, but at all events, the one great stumbling block is the violation of the prin- ciples of religious equality. The re-enact- ment of Church rat., by a private bill, has been happily removed. , We write in no spirit of undue exaltation over this triumphant defeat of a most unfair proposal, but we would fain call the attention of our readers to a few facts connected with the affair wh oh seem to us worth notice. The wails of Jericho have fallen down merely. by

_ - the blowing of a trumpet The oppontion had imoreely been organised, and only a few meetings held, yet this plan of subsidizing the Church of England out of the County ' rates had to be given up on the more state- ment of the facto at a public meeting. In the country papers of Saturday appeared the proceedings at Winetord, whore a moot. jag had been held, attended by no men of groat fortune or special influence, and whose resolutions were carried by a body principally of working men, and on Monday, such is the influence of public opinion, the Trustees felt themselves compelled to change a policy which had been deliberately agreed upon months ago, and had remained un- altered until that day. The effect of the meeting at Winsforil on the action of the Trustees wee that of the sun scattering a fog. What t hey had done and what they wished to do will not bear the light of day. For if we consider the eorupoeition of the Trustees present at that meeting on Mon- day we shall easily see that the vote mune from no great changes in their opinion as to the rectitude of the Measure, but simply from a conviction that it was certainly Ma- , politic end most probably impossible. There might have been three Nonconfor- mists present. There were certainly not half a dozen Liberals. The same men were there who originally voted for these clauses to be inserted, and yet no voice was raised for the retention of what a couple of months ago was thought both just and wise. How came this? Simply, we believe, from a fear . of public, opinion. And if this be the case, what a lesson does this teach us. We are told that the Church of England is so deeply I seated in the heart. of Englishmen that she can never cease to be a State Church. We are told that, except a few political None.- formiate, all wish her well, are willing to be taxed Mr her, are anzioue she shall hold a privileged position, and desire matters to go on as they do now. We are told that the working man is Conservative at heart, that he owes so much to the Church that has educated him, and watches over him from his baptism to his grave, that he will never desert her, or allow an impious hand to touch her. We are told that the Dissenters are in a miserable minority, and have no influence on the people as • body. And yet what has been the case here? Not one single objection was raised at Winsford to the resolution, though the meeting was declared open to all ratepayers, and the only dissent to it came from the parson of the church, who wrote a touching letter to a trustee, which Le published at full length, and the bearing of which was principally that he had asked to have his salary raised, and was answered by • " non-poesumus,“ and was in considerable danger each Sunday from plaster falling on his head. If the Church of England did live in the affections of the people, surely some one would have said that he was willing to pay an increased rate for the security of the portion's head. . If Diseent were so powerless, surely the local nil:Miterc would hhve been listened to with less respect than they were on that I occasion. But we do not wish to ascribe to the Wins- ford meeting only, this sudden change in part of the Trustees. he fact was that even when they hoped to carry this injustice with a high hand, they were conscious that it woe an injustice, and that it would nor stand the light of day. As long as the op- ponente were only two or three of their own number, who could, in the privacy of unre- ported proceedings, be snubbed and sneered at, they were willing enough to make the attempt ; but when the matter bad been debated and condemned outside, their hearts failed them. It was one thing to put down a brother Trustee or so, by force of vote, but a very different thing to force the Liberal press of the country. The bully is generally a coward, and though we are far from think- ing that all the Trustees who agreed to reverse their policy belong to either oft ese categories, there are some whom we would not hesitate to place in both. We are in- clined to believe that it would tend both to decorum and consistency if in future the Trustees would allow reporters tube present when they are voting away public money, so that they may be careful in their argued votes, and not be obliged to reverse them in such a hurry when their unfairness and im- policy has been discovered. It is at least more respectable to behave decently at once, and not to wait until public opinion has forced good behaviour upon you.

Tuna are at least two ways of putting a thing. You may call a spade a spade, or you may describe it in a more round-about way. So there are two ways of describing Lord Bee.conefield's habitual and wilful inac- curacy of aseertion. One is by using nearly the shortest word in our language, the other is by any amount of circumlocution you like. He signalised his second speech in the House of Lords by uttering three falsehoods. Two were pointed out and admitted in the House, and the third was mentioned in the papers by Mr. Gladstone. Their Lordships, who are, as a rule, truthful men and gentle- men, have not yet got accustomed to their new leader, and appear to have been some- what shocked. The House of Commons would have noticed without remark the three inaccuracies, or would have laughed at them. Nobody there expected Mr. Disraeli to be truthful. These lapses were called careless assertions, heedless rhetoric, forget- fulness, insufficient information, and so on, and it is a lamentable fact that a practice which if indulged in by any other member would have sent a shudder through the house, was, coming from the Prime Minister, considered a matter of course or a matter of mirth. But to come back to the way of putting things. The Daily Nara alluding to the epeech of Lord Beaconsfield, says : Lord Beaconsfield's explanations in the House of Lords on Thursday evening, about the outrages in Bulgaria partook of the inaccuracy which seems part of his mental constitution" This is very euphonious. The two sentences, that of the Daily News and that of Mr 04 onnell, mean and were intended to mean , exactly t e same thing.
